:question/worked-solution "We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{y}^{2}{csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}({csc}^{2}⁡x)({y}^{2})\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}{csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =[-\operatorname{cot}⁡x]_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\cdot {[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =(-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}))\cdot (\frac{{3}^{3}}{3}-\frac{{0}^{3}}{3}) \\  & =(0+1)\cdot (9-0) \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2b4c1a25-c7e8-5e0a-820b-a6b872059bec"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id ${∬}_{R}\frac{6+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[0,3]\times [1,2].$" :question/worked-solution "Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{6+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{6}{{y}^{2}}+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{6}{{y}^{2}}\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{6}{{y}^{2}}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(3-0){\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{6}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =3\cdot (-\frac{6}{y}{|}_{1}^{2}) \\  & =-18(\frac{1}{2}-1) \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A & =(2-1){\int }_{0}^{3}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{{3}^{3}}{3}-0 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{6+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A=9+9=18.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d9a8646d-83af-52fd-a349-459e6460b606"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d9a8646d-83af-52fd-a349-459e6460b606" :answer-field/id #uuid "d9a8646d-83af-52fd-a349-459e6460b606" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-22bea2a1-3640-54bb-b37a-5be01206ddd7" :answer-field/choices ["answer-4a778fe7-65d5-579b-bbd4-ac73193b8148" "answer-22bea2a1-3640-54bb-b37a-5be01206ddd7" "answer-842cd6fa-cc72-5447-a959-3164db0ba831" "answer-948fb597-3610-520a-bb28-3ef09776ffb8" "answer-1f7f1c17-e012-579b-b10d-42979ace1885"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4a778fe7-65d5-579b-bbd4-ac73193b8148" :answer/id #uuid "4a778fe7-65d5-579b-bbd4-ac73193b8148" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "12" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-22bea2a1-3640-54bb-b37a-5be01206ddd7" :answer/id #uuid "22bea2a1-3640-54bb-b37a-5be01206ddd7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "18" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-842cd6fa-cc72-5447-a959-3164db0ba831" :answer/id #uuid "842cd6fa-cc72-5447-a959-3164db0ba831" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "24" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-948fb597-3610-520a-bb28-3ef09776ffb8" :answer/id #uuid "948fb597-3610-520a-bb28-3ef09776ffb8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "36" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1f7f1c17-e012-579b-b10d-42979ace1885" :answer/id #uuid "1f7f1c17-e012-579b-b10d-42979ace1885" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "9" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-c07dad32-9851-5aba-9075-fbf7d573fb0f" :question/id #uuid "c07dad32-9851-5aba-9075-fbf7d573fb0f" :question/math-academy-id "q-81247" :question/problem "![](images/bc/bcc2eb6cd27450375016677390700675e9733c03dfd2c0100622e6f8c7d18e78.png)

${∬}_{R}\frac{6+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[0,3]\times [1,2].$"] ["question-c4bacfe6-30e7-5d9e-a1c2-df77375c3f7b" :question/worked-solution "Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{6+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{6}{{y}^{2}}+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{6}{{y}^{2}}\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{6}{{y}^{2}}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(3-0){\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{6}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =3\cdot (-\frac{6}{y}{|}_{1}^{2}) \\  & =-18(\frac{1}{2}-1) \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A & =(2-1){\int }_{0}^{3}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{{3}^{3}}{3}-0 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{6+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A=9+9=18.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-c4bacfe6-30e7-5d9e-a1c2-df77375c3f7b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-d9a8646d-83af-52fd-a349-459e6460b606" :answer-field/id #uuid of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

$$
\eqalign{
\iint\limits_{R}  xy\  e^{x+y}\: \textrm d A &= \iint\limits_{R} \Big( x\ \! e^x \Big)\Big( y\ \! e^{y} \Big) \textrm d A\[5pt]
&= \left(\int_0^1x\  e^{x}  \ \textrm d x\right)\left( \int_1^2 y \ \!e^{y} \ \textrm d y\right)\[5pt]
                                                                         &= \Big[x\ \!e^x-e^x\Big]_0^1 \cdot  \Big[y\ \!e^y-e^y\Big]_1^2\[5pt]
                                                                         &=  \Big(e^1-e^1 - \left(0-e^0\right)\Big) \cdot \Big(2e^2-e^2 - \left(e^1-e^1\right) \Big)\[5pt]
                                                                         &= 1\cdot e^2\[5pt]
                                                                         &= e^2
}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129845 :question/id #uuid "a8826be0-32c0-5213-809c-c90ea8221b73" :question/math-academy-id "q-71932"} {:db/id 17592186129846 :question/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3)\text{ }\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}3\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's evaluate each of the three integrals.

- The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(4-2){\int }_{-1}^{3}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{x}^{3}}{3}{|}_{-1}^{3} \\  & =2(\frac{27}{3}+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{56}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(3-(-1)){\int }_{2}^{4}{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}y \\  & =4{\int }_{2}^{4}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =4\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{3}{|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{4}^{3}-\frac{4}{3}{2}^{3} \\  & =\frac{224}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The function under the third integral is a constant, so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}3\,\text{d}A=3\,\text{Area}(R)=3\cdot (2\cdot 4)=24.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3)\,\text{d}A=\frac{56}{3}-\frac{224}{3}+24=-32.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129847 :question/id #uuid "b0d5598a-38f3-5d02-b7bc-c18028d75e03" :question/math-academy-id "q-71991"} {:db/id 17592186129848 :question/id #uuid "Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1-3x{y}^{2}}{x}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{x}-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}3{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(3-2){\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|]_{1}^{e} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}3{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(e-1){\int }_{2}^{3}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =(e-1)[{y}^{3}]_{2}^{3} \\  & =(e-1)({3}^{3}-{2}^{3}) \\  & =19(e-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1-3x{y}^{2}}{x}\,\text{d}A=1-19(e-1)=20-19e.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186348423 :question/id #uuid "a3840370-2613-5223-99ab-f0ad1e415b85" :question/math-academy-id "q-80626" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129171 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "307bccb6-036f-51bb-99ce-327aad8dfdbe" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Double Integral When the Integrand Contains Only One Variable"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "33574ba8-3a68-52a4-a29c-cefd3e428f26" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186345796} {:answer/id #uuid "88335118-c9d5-54e9-9421-6b4f5e015107" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186346531} {:answer/id #uuid "8b64d300-35ac-5d4f-b0f0-df7f7ad345c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186346558} {:answer/id #uuid "ab6239a6-a7ec-58f7-8e02-311f1bd7d30c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186346845} {:answer/id #uuid "ff960c84-9159-57ba-a8e5-03395c0f4a78" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186347596}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "ab6239a6-a7ec-58f7-8e02-311f1bd7d30c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186346845} :answer-field/id #uuid "1d0f1daa-3bd2-5289-b634-a2841e1fd2bf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186347658}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Calculate ${∬}_{R}(2+2x-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[0,3]\times [0,2].$" :question/worked-solution "Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$

The function under the first integral is a constant, so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}2\,\text{d}A=2\,\text{Area}(R)=2\cdot (3\cdot 2)=12.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The function under the second integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}2x\,\text{d}A & =(2-0){\int }_{0}^{3}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot [{x}^{2}]_{0}^{3} \\  & =2({3}^{2}-(0)^{2}) \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the third integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}2y\,\text{d}A & =(3-0){\int }_{0}^{2}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =3\cdot [{y}^{3}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =3({2}^{3}-{0}^{3}) \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(2+2x-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A=12+18-24=6.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186348424 :question/id #uuid "3c76c336-dd88-5200-b5c5-bdf849ab058b" :question/math-academy-id "q-80627"} {:db/id 17592186348427 :question/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{3-4y{x}^{3}}{y}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{3}{y}-4{x}^{3})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{3}{y}\text{ }\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}4{x}^{3}\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{3}{y}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(2-1){\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{3}{y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[3\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|]_{1}^{e} \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(1) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}4{x}^{3}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(e-1){\int }_{1}^{2}4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(e-1)[{x}^{4}]_{1}^{2} \\  & =(e-1)({2}^{4}-{1}^{4}) \\  & =15(e-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{3-4y{x}^{3}}{y}\,\text{d}A=3-15(e-1)=18-15e.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351276 :question/id #uuid "352b1d48-69ca-594f-bb84-628e58baed6e" :question/math-academy-id "q-81245"} {:db/id 17592186362483 :question/id #uuid $$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A & =(8-0){\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =8\cdot (-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}{|}_{1}^{2}) \\  & =8\cdot (-\frac{1}{8}-(-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A & =(2-1){\int }_{0}^{8}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}{|}_{0}^{8} \\  & =\frac{{8}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2} \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1+y{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A=3+32=35.\end{aligned}

:topic/math-academy-id 2000} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186130030 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130375 :tutorial/content "Double integrals have properties that are similar to the properties of definite integrals of single-variable functions:

- **Linearity of Double Integrals.** Suppose that  $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ are continuous functions on a domain $D$ and that $\alpha, \beta$ are constants. Then, we have

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \left[\alpha f(x,y) + \beta g(x,y)\right] \ \textrm d A = \alpha\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y)   \ \textrm d A + \beta\iint\limits_{D} g(x,y)   \ \textrm d A.
$$

- **The Double Integral of Unity.** The integral of $f(x,y) = 1$ over a domain $D$ is simply the area of $D\mathbin{:}$

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D}  \ \textrm d A = \displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} 1 \cdot \textrm d A = \textrm{Area}\ \!(D).
$$

Other properties are more specific to double integrals. 

- **The Multiplicative Property of Double Integrals.** If $f(x)$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and $g(y)$ is continuous on $[c,d]$ then 

$$
\iint\limits_{R}  f(x)g(y) \ \textrm d A = \left(\int_a^b f(x)  \ \textrm d x\right)\left( \int_c^d g(y) \ \textrm d y\right),
$$

where $R= [a,b] \times [c,d].$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6158466e-1222-52a1-88ad-028b5c5832c5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3860 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "15730ddd-c579-5f89-bff8-85f42db15b97" :step/math-academy-id 22622 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130031}} {:db/id 17592186130031 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129170 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128989 :question/id #uuid "53185b25-c690-500a-9a82-c18b37668e27" :question/math-academy-id "e-6106"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ec44686a-601b-52b3-81df-e57e6708fb93" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050207}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129845} {:db/id 17592186129846} {:db/id 17592186265786} {:db/id 17592186265787} {:db/id 17592186348401} {:db/id 17592186348403} {:db/id 17592186380852} {:db/id 17592186380859} {:db/id 17592186380866} {:db/id 17592186382393}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Double Integral Using the Multiplicative Property"} :step/id #uuid "2526c89c-75e6-5851-84b4-83ae4eaabc04" :step/math-academy-id 22623 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130032}} {:db/id 17592186130032 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130376 :tutorial/content "We can also apply the multiplicative property when the integrand contains only one of the variables. 

For example, suppose that $R= [a,b] \times [c,d].$ Then, we have the general result

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(f(x))(1)\,\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{c}^{d}1\,\text{d}y) \\  & =({\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x)(d-c) \\  & =(d-c){\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

 

By the same reasoning, we also have 

$$
\iint\limits_{R}  g(y) \, \textrm{d}A = (b-a) \int_c^d g(y) \, \textrm{d}y.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3acdc936-b0cf-5aca-a57a-00bdc558bb88" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3861 :tutorial/title "Applying the Multiplicative Property when the Integrand Contains Only One Variable"} :step/math-academy-id 22627} {:db/id 17592186130068 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130397 :tutorial/content "Remember that the definite integral of a single-variable function can be split up over adjacent subintervals. That is to say,

$$
\int_a^c f(x) \, \textrm dx = \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx + \int_b^c f(x) \, \textrm dx.
$$

In the same way, the definite integral of a two-variable function can be split up over adjacent sub-domains.

Suppose that a domain $D$ is the union of two adjacent sub-domains $D_1$ and $D_2$ (meaning that $D_1$ and $D_2$ are non-overlapping regions that could share a common border). Then, we have

$$
\iint\limits_{D}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A = \iint\limits_{D_1}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{D_2}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A.
$$

This property can be generalized if $D$ is split into a finite number $n$ of sub-domains (where $n>2$):

$$
\iint\limits_{D}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A = \iint\limits_{D_1}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{D_2}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A + \cdots + \iint\limits_{D_n}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bc4e2a2c-afd3-57e1-ac95-737c568153b8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4258 :tutorial/title "Additivity of Double Integrals"} :step/id #uuid "5249980b-32b5-5965-880e-a7948ef2b5f3" :step/math-academy-id 25886 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130069}} {:db/id 17592186130069 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129188 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186129007 :question/id #uuid "1c227b12-d40b-53a8-b568-b7bd380acbee" :question/math-academy-id "e-7023"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8505beff-75b8-57bf-9312-e0fcf32f44fd" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129873} {:db/id 17592186129874} {:db/id 17592186265799} {:db/id 17592186348431} {:db/id 17592186348432} {:db/id 17592186380887} {:db/id 17592186380894} {:db/id 17592186380901} {:db/id 17592186382455} {:db/id 17592186394030} {:db/id 17592186419654}] :knowledge-point/title "Using Additivity of Double Integrals"} :step/id #uuid "bca38320-513b-5017-88bb-f5d1a8c6013e" :step/math-academy-id 25887 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130070}} {:db/id 17592186130070 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130398 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we're integrating a single-variable function over a region $R.$ The definite integral of $f(x)$ over $R$ is not affected by whether the region $R$ is open or closed.

For example, consider the function $f(x) = 1,$ and define the regions $R = [0,1]$ and $R' = (0,1).$ Integrating $f(x)$ over $R$ and $R'$ gives the same result:

$$
\int_R f(x) \,\textrm d x = \int_{R'} f(x) \,\textrm d x = \int_{0}^1 \,\textrm d x = 1
$$

Intuitively, this is true because the rectangles formed by $f(x),$ namely $[0, 1]\times [0,1]$ and $(0, 1)\times (0,1),$ have the same area. 

We have a similar property for double integrals too. We can either include or exclude the boundaries of the integration regions without affecting the result. 

For example, the double integral of $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ over both $R=[0,1] \times [0,1]$ and over $R'=(0,1) \times (0,1)$ will give the same result:

$$
\iint\limits_{\large R} (x^2+y^2) \ \text{d}A = \iint\limits_{\large R'} (x^2+y^2) \ \text{d}A= \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{1} (x^2+y^2) \ \text{d}A
$$

Intuitively, this is true because the *volumes* of the shapes formed by $f(x,y)$ over the regions $R$ and $R'$ are the same.

Moreover, we'd get the same result if we were to integrate $f(x,y)$ over any of the following regions:

$$
(0,1] \times [0,1], \quad [0,1) \times [0,1], \quad (0,1) \times [0,1], \quad \ldots
$$

The same idea applies to double-integrals over non-rectangular boundaries, too." :tutorial/id #uuid "7f51d452-a229-5d76-885e-0fe84f787707" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4311 :tutorial/title "Open and Closed Regions of Integration"} :step/id #uuid "45710b0f-af68-5a20-b9ce-c5ecc560f4e5" :step/math-academy-id 26202 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130034}}] :activity/title "Properties of Double Integrals" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186129345} {:db/id 17592186130030 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130375 :tutorial/content "Double integrals have properties that are similar to the properties of definite integrals of single-variable functions:

- **Linearity of Double Integrals.** Suppose that  $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ are continuous functions on a domain $D$ and that $\alpha, \beta$ are constants. Then, we have

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \left[\alpha f(x,y) + \beta g(x,y)\right] \ \textrm d A = \alpha\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y)   \ \textrm d A + \beta\iint\limits_{D} g(x,y)   \ \textrm d A.
$$

$$

That is to say,

$$
\int_a^c f(x) \, \textrm dx = \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx + \int_b^c f(x) \, \textrm dx.
$$

In the same way, the definite integral of a two-variable function can be split up over adjacent sub-domains.

Suppose that a domain $D$ is the union of two adjacent sub-domains $D_1$ and $D_2$ (meaning that $D_1$ and $D_2$ are non-overlapping regions that could share a common border). Then, we have

$$
\iint\limits_{D}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A = \iint\limits_{D_1}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{D_2}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A.
$$

This property can be generalized if $D$ is split into a finite number $n$ of sub-domains (where $n>2$):

$$
\iint\limits_{D}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A = \iint\limits_{D_1}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{D_2}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A + \cdots + \iint\limits_{D_n}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bc4e2a2c-afd3-57e1-ac95-737c568153b8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4258 :tutorial/title "Additivity of Double Integrals"} :step/id #uuid "5249980b-32b5-5965-880e-a7948ef2b5f3" :step/math-academy-id 25886 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130069}} {:db/id 17592186130034 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129172 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128991 :question/id #uuid "0cb8fa8a-5be1-5f53-bfde-5acf325f6332" :question/math-academy-id "e-6108"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8059a197-e9fb-5306-8eed-62c0cea88f33" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049534} {:db/id 17592186050432}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129849} {:db/id 17592186129872} {:db/id 17592186265804} {:db/id 17592186265805} {:db/id 17592186265807} {:db/id 17592186265808} {:db/id 17592186351279} {:db/id 17592186380908} {:db/id 17592186382193} {:db/id 17592186382462}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Double Integral Using the Additivity Over a Rectangular Domain"} :step/id #uuid "f422ea91-80bb-5373-9f64-444e0646074d" :step/math-academy-id 22627} {:db/id 17592186130397 :tutorial/content "Remember that the definite integral of a single-variable function can be split up over adjacent subintervals. For example, consider the function $f(x) = 1,$ and define the regions $R = [0,1]$ and $R' = (0,1).$ Integrating $f(x)$ over $R$ and $R'$ gives the same result:

$$
\int_R f(x) \,\textrm d x = \int_{R'} f(x) \,\textrm d x = \int_{0}^1 \,\textrm d x = 1
$$

Intuitively, this is true because the rectangles formed by $f(x),$ namely $[0, 1]\times [0,1]$ and $(0, 1)\times (0,1),$ have the same area. 

We have a similar property for double integrals too. We can either include or exclude the boundaries of the integration regions without affecting the result. 

For example, the double integral of $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ over both $R=[0,1] \times [0,1]$ and over $R'=(0,1) \times (0,1)$ will give the same result:

$$
\iint\limits_{\large R} (x^2+y^2) \ \text{d}A = \iint\limits_{\large R'} (x^2+y^2) \ \text{d}A= \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{1} (x^2+y^2) \ \text{d}A
$$

Intuitively, this is true because the *volumes* of the shapes formed by $f(x,y)$ over the regions $R$ and $R'$ are the same.

Moreover, we'd get the same result if we were to integrate $f(x,y)$ over any of the following regions:

$$
(0,1] \times [0,1], \quad [0,1) \times [0,1], \quad (0,1) \times [0,1], \quad \ldots
$$

The same idea applies to double-integrals over non-rectangular boundaries, too." :tutorial/id #uuid "7f51d452-a229-5d76-885e-0fe84f787707" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4311 :tutorial/title "Open and Closed Regions of Integration"} :step/id #uuid "45710b0f-af68-5a20-b9ce-c5ecc560f4e5" :step/math-academy-id 26202 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130034}} {:db/id 17592186130398 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we're integrating a single-variable function over a region $R.$ The definite integral of $f(x)$ over $R$ is not affected by whether the region $R$ is open or closed.

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1-3x{y}^{2}}{x}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{x}-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}3{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(3-2){\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|]_{1}^{e} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}3{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(e-1){\int }_{2}^{3}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =(e-1)[{y}^{3}]_{2}^{3} \\  & =(e-1)({3}^{3}-{2}^{3}) \\  & =19(e-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1-3x{y}^{2}}{x}\,\text{d}A=1-19(e-1)=20-19e.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8b0d3e0f-96a8-599d-92f9-04874e8f5b73" :step/next {:db/id 17592186419656}} {:db/id 17592186419656 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129873 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "60fb41e7-e3b3-596b-9de2-56afe6dd5f07" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{∬}_{S}x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A" :db/id 17592186346193} {:answer/id #uuid "6c9ef82d-4456-5d25-ad26-90ed8d7f4c1f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{∬}_{S}x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A" :db/id 17592186346295} {:answer/id #uuid "705f8690-2e07-5932-b07c-8089792360e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{∬}_{T}x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A" :db/id 17592186346333} {:answer/id #uuid "9666eb71-130a-59fc-8098-2ba78743d703" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{∬}_{S}x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}y\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A" :db/id 17592186346666} {:answer/id #uuid "c006f721-3d51-5d16-a6a8-1b8222268571" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{∬}_{S}x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}(x+{x}^{2}y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A" :db/id 17592186347011}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186346193} :answer-field/id #uuid "8ef450e5-1471-5ba8-8652-38a2e4337160" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186347853}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3e01cd29-3b44-5c08-bc75-551f046b44dd" :question/math-academy-id "q-80452" :question/problem "![](images/ed/ed0be2aca8d43d733e91f3a8feaaca0649957dcbd516a8218b1e7dea136170d8.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1-3x{y}^{2}}{x}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{x}-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}3{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(3-2){\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|]_{1}^{e} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}3{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(e-1){\int }_{2}^{3}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =(e-1)[{y}^{3}]_{2}^{3} \\  & =(e-1)({3}^{3}-{2}^{3}) \\  & =19(e-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1-3x{y}^{2}}{x}\,\text{d}A=1-19(e-1)=20-19e.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8b0d3e0f-96a8-599d-92f9-04874e8f5b73" :step/next {:db/id 17592186419656}} {:db/id 17592186419656 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129873 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "60fb41e7-e3b3-596b-9de2-56afe6dd5f07" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{∬}_{S}x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A" :db/id 17592186346193} {:answer/id #uuid "6c9ef82d-4456-5d25-ad26-90ed8d7f4c1f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{∬}_{S}x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A" :db/id 17592186346295} {:answer/id #uuid "705f8690-2e07-5932-b07c-8089792360e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{∬}_{T}x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A" :db/id 17592186346333} {:answer/id #uuid "9666eb71-130a-59fc-8098-2ba78743d703" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{∬}_{S}x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}y\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A" :db/id 17592186346666} {:answer/id #uuid "c006f721-3d51-5d16-a6a8-1b8222268571" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{∬}_{S}x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}(x+{x}^{2}y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A" :db/id 17592186347011}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186346193} :answer-field/id #uuid "8ef450e5-1471-5ba8-8652-38a2e4337160" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186347853}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3e01cd29-3b44-5c08-bc75-551f046b44dd" :question/math-academy-id "q-80452" :question/problem "![](images/ed/ed0be2aca8d43d733e91f3a8feaaca0649957dcbd516a8218b1e7dea136170d8.png)

17592186045417] [17592186046658 1008 "Our Mathematics for Machine Learning course provides a comprehensive foundation of the essential mathematical tools required to study modern machine learning.
This course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.
On completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.
Students then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.
As part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.
Students will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data.
The course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data.
A solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks.
Students also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.
Students work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.
On the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.
Students extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.
The course concludes with parametric inference, focusing on point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals, which form the statistical foundation for many machine learning Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.
Students learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.
Students then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.
The course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.
The course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.
Students then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.
The final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. The course concludes with second-order linear differential equations and oscillatory systems, including harmonic motion, damped oscillators, and resonance—fundamental mathematical models for vibrating
